Sec. №00

What this lecture covers

Think of this as the lecture where forces stop being the main characters and energy takes the stage.

We motivate the energy-based view of robot dynamics, then build it up piece by piece. First we contrast force methods (Newton–Euler) with energy methods (Lagrangian) and argue why the latter scales better for multi-link manipulators. Next we revisit kinetic and potential energy for chains of rigid bodies, where velocity coupling makes things genuinely interesting.

We introduce generalised coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler–Lagrange equations. We then show how velocity kinematics — Jacobians, angular-velocity sums along the chain — feed into a matrix form for kinetic energy. Finally we derive the standard manipulator equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ and identify the physical role of each term.

Objective sheet
Learning objectives

Understand energy in multi-link systems, the Lagrangian framework, why energy beats force methods, generalised coordinates, the Euler–Lagrange equations, and how to derive dynamic equations for any robot configuration.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 00 → 01 —
Sec. №01

Why energy methods beat force methods for robots

Energy is a scalar. That single fact is why this whole approach scales so much better than force balances.

Force-based and energy-based approaches are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same equations of motion — but the path to those equations is very different. For a single pendulum, Newton's second law and a free-body diagram are perfectly natural. For a 3-DOF arm with three coupled links, every joint introduces constraint forces, every link needs its own force and moment balance, and vector bookkeeping in shifting coordinate frames becomes a frequent source of sign errors.

The Lagrangian approach replaces vectors with scalars. We compute the total kinetic and potential energy of the system, form $L = T - V$, and let the Euler–Lagrange machinery extract the equations of motion. Constraint forces at the joints — which do no work — drop out automatically. The procedure is the same for every robot, which makes it well suited to symbolic computation and code generation.

Method A
Force-based (Newton–Euler)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector equations in multiple frames. Powerful, but error-prone as the chain grows.

Method B
Energy-based (Lagrangian)

Scalar kinetic and potential energies, one Lagrangian, a systematic differentiation recipe. Constraint forces vanish; coupling appears in $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ for free.

Case in point
3-DOF arm, two routes

Newton–Euler: 6 force/moment equations per link plus constraint forces, all coupled. Lagrangian: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L$, one mechanical recipe.

Now drive the comparison yourself. Pick which formulation you want to apply to a 3-DOF arm and watch the bookkeeping stack up on one side and collapse on the other.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 01 → 02 —
Sec. №02

Kinetic energy of a multi-link manipulator

Translation, rotation, and coupling across links — kinetic energy in a manipulator hides all of robotics' interesting dynamics.

In a manipulator, kinetic energy is not just $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ for a point mass. Every link generally translates and rotates, and the motion of joint $j$ feeds into the velocity of every link further out along the chain. That coupling is the source of all the interesting cross-terms we will see later in $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

For a robot with $n$ links, the total kinetic energy is

$$T = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i\, \mathbf{v}_i^{T} \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^{T} \mathbf{I}_i\, \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right],$$

where $m_i$ is the mass of link $i$, $\mathbf{v}_i$ the linear velocity of its centre of mass, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ its angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ its inertia tensor about the centre of mass.

The key point is that both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ are functions of the joint variables $\mathbf{q}$ and joint velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$. Once we express them in terms of $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, $T$ becomes a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ — which is exactly what we need for the inertia matrix.

Decomposition
Two contributions per link

Translational $\tfrac{1}{2}m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T\mathbf{v}_i$ from the centre-of-mass motion, plus rotational $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ about the centre of mass.

Key insight
Velocity coupling

$\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on all joints from the base out to link $i$. That dependency is where the inertial coupling between joints is born.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 02 → 03 —
Sec. №03

Potential energy and configuration-dependent gravity

Potential energy is the easy half: position in, scalar out.

Potential energy in standard manipulators is almost always gravitational. Unlike kinetic energy, it depends only on positions — not on velocities — which makes it much easier to compute.

For a uniform gravitational field, the total potential energy is

$$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i\, \mathbf{g}^{T} \mathbf{r}_i,$$

where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^{T}\ \text{m/s}^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the position of link $i$'s centre of mass.

Because $\mathbf{r}_i$ depends on the configuration, $V$ does too. An arm stretched out horizontally stores far more potential energy than the same arm folded vertically; the difference is exactly the gravitational torque your actuators must overcome to hold a pose. The choice of reference height is arbitrary — only differences matter — so pick a frame that keeps the algebra clean.

Forward link
Why we care

$\partial V / \partial q_i$ becomes the gravity term $c_i(\mathbf{q})$ in the final manipulator equation — the static torque needed just to hold a configuration.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 03 → 04 —
Sec. №04

The Lagrangian and the Euler–Lagrange equations

One scalar, four derivatives per joint, and you are done. That is the contract.

Generalised coordinates are any independent set of variables that completely specify the configuration. For a manipulator, the joint variables $\mathbf{q} = (q_1, \ldots, q_n)$ — angles for revolute joints, displacements for prismatic ones — are the natural choice. They are minimal, they automatically respect the kinematic constraints, and they map directly onto actuator outputs.

The Lagrangian is

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q}).$$

Physically, $L$ measures the excess of kinetic over potential energy. The principle of least action tells us that physical motions extremise the time integral of $L$, and the resulting condition is the Euler–Lagrange equations:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n,$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalised force on coordinate $q_i$ (joint torque for revolute, joint force for prismatic).

This gives a recipe: write $T$ and $V$ in terms of $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, form $L = T - V$, take the partial derivatives, and you have the equations of motion.

Euler–Lagrange equation, component formd/dt (∂L/∂q̇_i) − ∂L/∂q_i = τ_i,    i = 1, …, n
Coord. choice
Why joint variables are the right coordinates

They give a minimal description, they automatically satisfy joint constraints, and they correspond to what the controller actually commands.

Procedure
The recipe

1. Write $T(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ and $V(\mathbf{q})$. 2. Form $L = T - V$. 3. Compute $\partial L/\partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L/\partial q_i$. 4. Apply the Euler–Lagrange equation for each $i$. 5. Tidy up.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 04 → 05 —
Sec. №05

Worked walkthrough: a 2-DOF planar arm

Two joints, and we are already meeting Coriolis and centrifugal terms. Welcome to robot dynamics.

Consider a 2-DOF planar manipulator with revolute joints, link lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$, masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, and centre-of-mass inertias $I_1$ and $I_2$.

Step 1 — Coordinates. Take $q_1 = \theta_1$ as the angle of the first link relative to the base, and $q_2 = \theta_2$ as the angle of the second link relative to the first.

Step 2 — Kinetic energy. Each link contributes translational kinetic energy from its centre-of-mass velocity plus rotational kinetic energy. Link 1 rotates with angular velocity $\dot{\theta}_1$. Link 2 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2$, and its centre of mass has a velocity that mixes both joint rates — so $T$ contains a cross-term in $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$. This cross-term is exactly the inertial coupling between the two joints.

Step 3 — Potential energy. The height of each centre of mass depends on $\theta_1$ (and, for link 2, on $\theta_2$ as well). $V$ is therefore a configuration-dependent sum of gravity terms.

Step 4 — Euler–Lagrange. Apply the equation for $i = 1$ and $i = 2$. You will get two coupled, nonlinear ODEs containing inertial terms, Coriolis/centrifugal terms (from the $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ and $\dot{\theta}_j^2$ structure), and gravitational terms.

Even this minimal example shows the texture of all manipulator dynamics: the inertia matrix is configuration-dependent, the joints are inertially coupled, and gravity loads vary with pose.

Pay attention
Where the coupling enters

Link 2's centre-of-mass velocity depends on both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$. Squaring that velocity in $T$ produces the cross-term $\dot{\theta}_1\dot{\theta}_2$ — the off-diagonal entries of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

First, sweep the elbow angle and watch the $2\times 2$ inertia matrix breathe. The off-diagonal $D_{12}$ should collapse to exactly $m_2 L_2^2$ when link 2 sits perpendicular to link 1 — the special case from homework Task 4.

Then take the wheel yourself. Type a Lagrangian for the 2-DOF arm (or load the homework template), let the playground apply Euler–Lagrange symbolically, and watch the resulting trajectory simulate. Edit a term — the equations and the motion both update.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 05 → 06 —
Sec. №06

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Every revolute joint adds itself to every link downstream. Once you see that, you can write angular velocities by inspection.

To turn $T$ into a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, we need explicit expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ in terms of joint velocities.

Linear velocity. If the centre of mass of link $i$ has position $\mathbf{r}_i(\mathbf{q})$, then by the chain rule

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_1}\dot{q}_1 + \cdots + \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_i}\dot{q}_i = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}},$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the linear-velocity Jacobian for that centre of mass.

Angular velocity. For a revolute joint $j$, every link beyond joint $j$ in the chain picks up $\dot{q}_j$ in its angular velocity. Prismatic joints contribute nothing. The total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between the base and link $i$.

For a 3-DOF planar arm: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$ — each successive link is driven by more joints, so the kinetic energy gets steadily richer in coupling terms.

Angular velocities of a 3-DOF planar revolute armω₁ = q̇₁
ω₂ = q̇₁ + q̇₂
ω₃ = q̇₁ + q̇₂ + q̇₃
Definition
Two Jacobians per link

$\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ maps $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ to the linear velocity of link $i$'s centre of mass; the rotational Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\omega i}$ does the same for $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$.

Build it yourself. Drag joint-rate contributions onto each link until $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1, \boldsymbol{\omega}_2, \boldsymbol{\omega}_3$ pick up exactly the joints upstream of them. The win condition encodes the rule that lets you write angular velocities by inspection.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 06 → 07 —
Sec. №07

Kinetic energy in matrix form: the inertia matrix

The inertia matrix is the kinetic energy's fingerprint. Everything that makes robot dynamics nonlinear lives inside $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into $T$, the total kinetic energy becomes a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^{T} \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}},$$

where the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ has entries

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^{T}\!\left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^{T} \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right].$$

Reading this physically: $D_{ii}$ is the effective inertia seen by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves, while the off-diagonal entries $D_{ij}$ encode inertial coupling between joints. $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — symmetry follows from the construction, and positive definiteness follows from the fact that kinetic energy is positive whenever the robot is moving.

The configuration dependence of $\mathbf{D}$ is the reason robot dynamics are nonlinear: as the arm changes posture, the effective inertia changes, and so does the coupling between joints.

Spec
Three properties to remember

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent. The first two guarantee a sane physics; the third is what makes the dynamics nonlinear.

Structure
Diagonal vs off-diagonal

Diagonals = effective inertia of each joint in isolation. Off-diagonals = inertial coupling — torque applied at joint $j$ shows up as acceleration at joint $i$.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 07 → 08 —
Sec. №08

From the Lagrangian to the manipulator equation

The whole module collapses to one line: $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$. Memorise it; we will use it everywhere.

We now apply the Euler–Lagrange equations to $L = T - V$ using $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$.

Step 1 — Velocity derivative.

$$\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = \sum_{j} D_{ij}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{q}_j.$$

Step 2 — Take $d/dt$. Because $\mathbf{D}$ depends on $\mathbf{q}$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) = \sum_{j} D_{ij}\, \ddot{q}_j + \sum_{j,k} \frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k}\, \dot{q}_k \dot{q}_j.$$

Step 3 — Position derivatives.

$$\frac{\partial T}{\partial q_i} = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{j,k} \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\, \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k, \qquad \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_i} = c_i(\mathbf{q}).$$

Step 4 — Assemble. Substituting into the Euler–Lagrange equation and collecting terms gives, for each $i$,

$$\sum_{j} D_{ij}(\mathbf{q})\, \ddot{q}_j + h_i(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + c_i(\mathbf{q}) = \tau_i,$$

or in compact matrix form

$$\boxed{\;\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}\;}.$$

This is the equation of robot dynamics. Every algorithm in the rest of the course — inverse dynamics, computed-torque control, simulation — is built on it.

Standard formD(q) q̈ + h(q, q̇) + c(q) = τ
Headline result
Standard manipulator equation

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ — inertia × acceleration, plus velocity-coupling terms, plus gravity, equals applied joint torque.

Drive the derivation yourself, one rule at a time. The widget shows the current expression and a menu of production rules; pick the one Euler–Lagrange actually needs next and the next line unlocks.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 08 → 09 —
Sec. №09

Anatomy of the manipulator equation: $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$

Three terms, three stories: inertia, motion-coupling, gravity. Keep them straight and the equations of motion stop being scary.

The Lagrangian derivation naturally splits the equation of motion into three physically meaningful pieces.

Inertia $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$. Comes from $T$. Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Its diagonal entries are the effective inertias of each joint; off-diagonals carry the inertial coupling.

Coriolis and centrifugal terms $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$. Come from the time derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ and from $\partial T/\partial \mathbf{q}$. They are quadratic in joint velocities:

$$h_i(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) = \sum_{j,k} h_{ijk}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k, \quad h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right).$$

The symbols $h_{ijk}$ are the Christoffel symbols of the first kind. Terms with $j = k$ are centrifugal (one joint moves, pushing another); terms with $j \neq k$ are Coriolis (two joints moving simultaneously produce a coupling).

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$. Comes from $V$:

$$c_i(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_i}.$$

This is the static torque the actuator must supply just to hold the arm against gravity at configuration $\mathbf{q}$.

Knowing which physical effect a given term represents is what lets you debug a derivation: if all your velocity-squared terms come out wrong, you have a problem in $\mathbf{h}$; if a stationary pose drifts in simulation, you have a problem in $\mathbf{c}$.

Term 1 of 3
$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ — inertia

Symmetric, positive definite. Comes straight from kinetic energy.

Term 2 of 3
$\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis / centrifugal

Quadratic in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$. Built from Christoffel symbols of $\mathbf{D}$. Zero when nothing is moving.

Term 3 of 3
$\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ — gravity

$c_i = \partial V/\partial q_i$. The static load you have to fight just to hold a pose.

Check your grip with four questions. Decide which term carries which physical effect, what vanishes when the robot is stationary, and where to look first when a simulation misbehaves. The distractors are the misreadings most often seen in coursework.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 09 → 10 —
Sec. №10

Why this matters in industry

Everything in Module 2 ends up baked into industrial controllers at 1 kHz. Treat it accordingly.

The Lagrangian formulation is not just a tidy piece of mathematics — it is what runs inside modern industrial robot controllers. Embedded controllers evaluate $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster and use them for computed-torque control, trajectory optimisation, collision detection by energy monitoring, and predictive maintenance.

A concrete example from automotive welding: a manufacturer replaced simple per-joint PID control with model-based control built on the Lagrangian dynamic model. Position error dropped from $\pm 2$ mm to $\pm 0.2$ mm, cycle times fell from 45 s to 28 s, and energy consumption dropped by around 25%. The whole improvement comes from the controller knowing, at every instant, what torque is needed for inertia, what is needed for Coriolis/centrifugal coupling, and what is needed for gravity — exactly the three terms we just derived.

That is the punchline of this module: the same scalar reasoning we used to write $L = T - V$ on paper is, almost literally, what is doing real-time computation on a factory robot.

Where deployed
Where the equation lives

Computed-torque control, model-predictive control, simulation, energy-based safety monitoring — all built on $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 10 → 11 —
Sec. №11

Module summary and what comes next

If you can explain why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, what $\mathbf{h}$ does when nothing is moving, and where $\mathbf{c}$ comes from, you are ready for Module 3.

We replaced free-body diagrams with energy. We wrote kinetic energy as $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, potential energy as $V = \sum m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$, and combined them into the Lagrangian $L = T - V$. The Euler–Lagrange equations then gave us the standard form

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau},$$

with every term physically meaningful and every step procedural.

Module 3 will take this same machinery and push it further: explicit velocity formulations along the kinematic chain, a systematic algorithm for assembling $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of the Coriolis/centrifugal block $\mathbf{h}$ via Christoffel symbols, and worked examples on real robot geometries.

Before moving on, make sure you are comfortable with: matrix calculus and partial derivatives of matrix expressions, position and velocity expressions from transformation matrices, dot/cross products and frame transformations, and kinetic and potential energy in multi-body systems.

Self-check
Conceptual check

Can you explain: why energy methods beat force methods for robots, what each term in $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ represents, how the Lagrangian handles constraint forces, and why manipulator dynamics are nonlinear and coupled?

Next sheet
Coming in Module 3

Lagrangian formulation for robot dynamics — full derivations for real geometries, velocity Jacobians along the chain, and the assembly of $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ in practice.

Practice — try these on your own

Small activities to test your grip on today's ideas. Try each one first, sketch as you go, then reveal the worked solution to compare. These are formative — nothing to hand in.

1 · Kinematics of a 2-DOF planar arm with tip masses

Consider a 2-link planar arm with revolute joints. Link 1 has length $L_1$ with point mass $m_1$ at its tip; link 2 has length $L_2$ with point mass $m_2$ at its tip. Joint angles $\theta_1$ (link 1 vs the horizontal $x$-axis) and $\theta_2$ (link 2 vs link 1) are measured in the usual way. Neglect distributed link mass and inertia.

Write the position vectors of $m_1$ and $m_2$ in the base frame as functions of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$. Then differentiate to get their velocities in terms of $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.

Self-check after you've tried
  • Your $\mathbf{r}_1$ should depend only on $L_1$ and $\theta_1$, not on $\theta_2$.
  • $\mathbf{r}_2$ should be the sum of two vectors of lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$ at angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ respectively.
  • After differentiating, $\mathbf{v}_1$ should be linear in $\dot{\theta}_1$; $\mathbf{v}_2$ should be linear in both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$.
Show worked solution

Positions. Tip of link 1:

$$\mathbf{r}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} L_1 \cos\theta_1 \\ L_1 \sin\theta_1 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Tip of link 2 (link 2 is at angle $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ in the base frame):

$$\mathbf{r}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} L_1 \cos\theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \end{bmatrix}.$$

Velocities. Differentiating with respect to time:

$$\mathbf{v}_1 = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -L_1 \sin\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 \\ \phantom{-}L_1 \cos\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 \end{bmatrix},$$ $$\mathbf{v}_2 = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -L_1 \sin\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 - L_2 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2) \\ \phantom{-}L_1 \cos\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2) \end{bmatrix}.$$

Notice that $\mathbf{v}_2$ involves both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ — that coupling is what will produce the off-diagonal entries of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ in the next task.

2 · Kinetic energy and the inertia matrix

Using the velocities you derived in Task 1, write the total kinetic energy $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 \|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2$ as a quadratic form in $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$. Read off the entries of the $2\times 2$ inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

Self-check after you've tried
  • $T$ should be a sum of $\dot{\theta}_1^2$, $\dot{\theta}_2^2$, and $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ terms — no other velocity products.
  • $\mathbf{D}$ must be symmetric: $D_{12} = D_{21}$.
  • At $\theta_2 = \pi/2$ (link 2 perpendicular to link 1), $\cos\theta_2 = 0$ and the off-diagonal entry should reduce to $m_2 L_2^2$.
Show worked solution

Squared magnitudes. Since point-mass tips have no rotational kinetic energy of their own, only $\tfrac{1}{2}m_i\|\mathbf{v}_i\|^2$ contributes.

$\|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2 = L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2$.

For $\mathbf{v}_2$, expand and use $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ on the $\theta_1$ and $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ pieces, with cross terms collapsing via $\cos(A)\cos(B) + \sin(A)\sin(B) = \cos(A - B)$:

$$\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2 = L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2).$$

Total kinetic energy.

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2).$$

Read off $\mathbf{D}$. Collect coefficients of $\dot{\theta}_1^2$, $\dot{\theta}_2^2$, and $\dot{\theta}_1\dot{\theta}_2$ in $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}$:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix} (m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 + m_2 L_2^2 + 2 m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 & m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \\ m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 & m_2 L_2^2 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Note $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric and depends on $\theta_2$ only — the explicit configuration-dependence of the effective inertia.

3 · Potential energy and the Lagrangian

Take gravity acting in $-y$. Write the gravitational potential energy $V$ of the two tip masses as a function of $\theta_1, \theta_2$. Then form the Lagrangian $L = T - V$ using your $T$ from Task 2.

Self-check after you've tried
  • $V$ should depend on $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ but not on the joint velocities.
  • $V$ should be zero when both link tips sit on the $x$-axis ($\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 0$).
  • Inspect the partial $\partial V/\partial \theta_1$: it should give a gravity-torque term that vanishes when the arm hangs straight down.
Show worked solution

Heights of the tip masses. From the position expressions in Task 1, the $y$-coordinates are

$$y_1 = L_1 \sin\theta_1, \qquad y_2 = L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

Potential energy. With $g$ the magnitude of gravity and reference height at $y = 0$,

$$V = m_1 g\, y_1 + m_2 g\, y_2 = (m_1 + m_2) g L_1 \sin\theta_1 + m_2 g L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

Lagrangian. Using $T$ from Task 2,

$$L = T - V = \tfrac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)$$ $$\qquad - (m_1 + m_2) g L_1 \sin\theta_1 - m_2 g L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

This Lagrangian is everything the Euler–Lagrange machinery needs. From here, applying $\frac{d}{dt}(\partial L/\partial \dot{\theta}_i) - \partial L/\partial \theta_i = \tau_i$ for $i = 1, 2$ produces the two coupled equations of motion of the 2-DOF arm.

4 · Verify symmetry and a special case of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Take the inertia matrix from Task 2 and verify two things by hand: (a) $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is symmetric for all $\theta_2$, and (b) when $\theta_2 = \pm \pi/2$, the inertial coupling $D_{12}$ reduces to a purely geometric expression in $m_2$ and $L_2$ — write down what it becomes and explain physically why the $L_1$ contribution disappears in that pose.

Self-check after you've tried
  • After substituting $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, you should get $D_{12} = m_2 L_2^2$.
  • The disappearance of $L_1$ must be tied to the geometry of link 2's velocity contribution from joint 1 in that pose — try sketching the arm at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$.
  • Symmetry should follow from the construction of $T$ as $\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D} \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ — there is no way to tell $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ apart from $\dot{\theta}_2 \dot{\theta}_1$.
Show worked solution

(a) Symmetry. From Task 2,

$$D_{12}(\mathbf{q}) = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2, \qquad D_{21}(\mathbf{q}) = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2.$$

These are identical for every $\theta_2$, so $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})^T$. Symmetry is structural: $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ only sees the symmetric part of $\mathbf{D}$, so we can — and do — take $\mathbf{D}$ symmetric without loss of generality.

(b) Special case $\theta_2 = \pi/2$. Then $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, and

$$D_{12} = m_2 L_2^2 + 0 = m_2 L_2^2.$$

The physical picture: at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, link 2 sticks out perpendicular to link 1. When joint 1 moves, the component of $m_2$'s motion that is aligned with the motion driven by joint 2 reduces to the motion at distance $L_2$ from joint 2's axis — the $L_1$ contribution to $\mathbf{v}_2$ is perpendicular to the joint-2 contribution and so does not couple into the $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ cross-term.

In short: the off-diagonal of $\mathbf{D}$ measures how much joint 1's motion helps joint 2's motion in $T$. At $\theta_2 = \pi/2$ that overlap is purely $m_2 L_2^2$, the same value as $D_{22}$ itself.

Lecture 02 · Module 2 · Robot Manipulator Dynamics

Energy-Based Approach
to Robot Dynamics

Lagrangian mechanics as a systematic route from kinetic and potential energy to the equations of motion of a manipulator.

Drawing
RMD-02
In this module we step away from free-body diagrams and learn to think about a manipulator as a scalar — its kinetic and potential energy. Once we have those two numbers as functions of the joint variables, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$ and the Euler–Lagrange equations do the bookkeeping for us. The payoff is enormous: constraint forces disappear, coupling between joints emerges naturally, and the same recipe works whether you have a 2-DOF planar arm or a 7-DOF industrial robot.

Sec. №00

What this lecture covers

Think of this as the lecture where forces stop being the main characters and energy takes the stage.

We motivate the energy-based view of robot dynamics, then build it up piece by piece. First we contrast force methods (Newton–Euler) with energy methods (Lagrangian) and argue why the latter scales better for multi-link manipulators. Next we revisit kinetic and potential energy for chains of rigid bodies, where velocity coupling makes things genuinely interesting.

We introduce generalised coordinates, the Lagrangian $L = T - V$, and the Euler–Lagrange equations. We then show how velocity kinematics — Jacobians, angular-velocity sums along the chain — feed into a matrix form for kinetic energy. Finally we derive the standard manipulator equation $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ and identify the physical role of each term.

Objective sheet
Learning objectives

Understand energy in multi-link systems, the Lagrangian framework, why energy beats force methods, generalised coordinates, the Euler–Lagrange equations, and how to derive dynamic equations for any robot configuration.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 00 → 01 —
Sec. №01

Why energy methods beat force methods for robots

Energy is a scalar. That single fact is why this whole approach scales so much better than force balances.

Force-based and energy-based approaches are mathematically equivalent — they produce the same equations of motion — but the path to those equations is very different. For a single pendulum, Newton's second law and a free-body diagram are perfectly natural. For a 3-DOF arm with three coupled links, every joint introduces constraint forces, every link needs its own force and moment balance, and vector bookkeeping in shifting coordinate frames becomes a frequent source of sign errors.

The Lagrangian approach replaces vectors with scalars. We compute the total kinetic and potential energy of the system, form $L = T - V$, and let the Euler–Lagrange machinery extract the equations of motion. Constraint forces at the joints — which do no work — drop out automatically. The procedure is the same for every robot, which makes it well suited to symbolic computation and code generation.

Method A
Force-based (Newton–Euler)

Per-link free-body diagrams, explicit constraint forces, vector equations in multiple frames. Powerful, but error-prone as the chain grows.

Method B
Energy-based (Lagrangian)

Scalar kinetic and potential energies, one Lagrangian, a systematic differentiation recipe. Constraint forces vanish; coupling appears in $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ for free.

Case in point
3-DOF arm, two routes

Newton–Euler: 6 force/moment equations per link plus constraint forces, all coupled. Lagrangian: 3 scalar $T_i$, 3 scalar $V_i$, one $L$, one mechanical recipe.

Now drive the comparison yourself. Pick which formulation you want to apply to a 3-DOF arm and watch the bookkeeping stack up on one side and collapse on the other.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 01 → 02 —
Sec. №02

Kinetic energy of a multi-link manipulator

Translation, rotation, and coupling across links — kinetic energy in a manipulator hides all of robotics' interesting dynamics.

In a manipulator, kinetic energy is not just $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ for a point mass. Every link generally translates and rotates, and the motion of joint $j$ feeds into the velocity of every link further out along the chain. That coupling is the source of all the interesting cross-terms we will see later in $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

For a robot with $n$ links, the total kinetic energy is

$$T = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ m_i\, \mathbf{v}_i^{T} \mathbf{v}_i + \boldsymbol{\omega}_i^{T} \mathbf{I}_i\, \boldsymbol{\omega}_i \right],$$

where $m_i$ is the mass of link $i$, $\mathbf{v}_i$ the linear velocity of its centre of mass, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ its angular velocity, and $\mathbf{I}_i$ its inertia tensor about the centre of mass.

The key point is that both $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ are functions of the joint variables $\mathbf{q}$ and joint velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$. Once we express them in terms of $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, $T$ becomes a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ — which is exactly what we need for the inertia matrix.

Decomposition
Two contributions per link

Translational $\tfrac{1}{2}m_i \mathbf{v}_i^T\mathbf{v}_i$ from the centre-of-mass motion, plus rotational $\tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\omega}_i^T \mathbf{I}_i \boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ about the centre of mass.

Key insight
Velocity coupling

$\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ depend on all joints from the base out to link $i$. That dependency is where the inertial coupling between joints is born.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 02 → 03 —
Sec. №03

Potential energy and configuration-dependent gravity

Potential energy is the easy half: position in, scalar out.

Potential energy in standard manipulators is almost always gravitational. Unlike kinetic energy, it depends only on positions — not on velocities — which makes it much easier to compute.

For a uniform gravitational field, the total potential energy is

$$V = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i\, \mathbf{g}^{T} \mathbf{r}_i,$$

where $\mathbf{g}$ is the gravitational acceleration vector (typically $[0, 0, -9.81]^{T}\ \text{m/s}^2$) and $\mathbf{r}_i$ is the position of link $i$'s centre of mass.

Because $\mathbf{r}_i$ depends on the configuration, $V$ does too. An arm stretched out horizontally stores far more potential energy than the same arm folded vertically; the difference is exactly the gravitational torque your actuators must overcome to hold a pose. The choice of reference height is arbitrary — only differences matter — so pick a frame that keeps the algebra clean.

Forward link
Why we care

$\partial V / \partial q_i$ becomes the gravity term $c_i(\mathbf{q})$ in the final manipulator equation — the static torque needed just to hold a configuration.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 03 → 04 —
Sec. №04

The Lagrangian and the Euler–Lagrange equations

One scalar, four derivatives per joint, and you are done. That is the contract.

Generalised coordinates are any independent set of variables that completely specify the configuration. For a manipulator, the joint variables $\mathbf{q} = (q_1, \ldots, q_n)$ — angles for revolute joints, displacements for prismatic ones — are the natural choice. They are minimal, they automatically respect the kinematic constraints, and they map directly onto actuator outputs.

The Lagrangian is

$$L(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}, t) = T(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}) - V(\mathbf{q}).$$

Physically, $L$ measures the excess of kinetic over potential energy. The principle of least action tells us that physical motions extremise the time integral of $L$, and the resulting condition is the Euler–Lagrange equations:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i} = \tau_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n,$$

where $\tau_i$ is the generalised force on coordinate $q_i$ (joint torque for revolute, joint force for prismatic).

This gives a recipe: write $T$ and $V$ in terms of $\mathbf{q}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, form $L = T - V$, take the partial derivatives, and you have the equations of motion.

Euler–Lagrange equation, component formd/dt (∂L/∂q̇_i) − ∂L/∂q_i = τ_i,    i = 1, …, n
Coord. choice
Why joint variables are the right coordinates

They give a minimal description, they automatically satisfy joint constraints, and they correspond to what the controller actually commands.

Procedure
The recipe

1. Write $T(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ and $V(\mathbf{q})$. 2. Form $L = T - V$. 3. Compute $\partial L/\partial \dot{q}_i$ and $\partial L/\partial q_i$. 4. Apply the Euler–Lagrange equation for each $i$. 5. Tidy up.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 04 → 05 —
Sec. №05

Worked walkthrough: a 2-DOF planar arm

Two joints, and we are already meeting Coriolis and centrifugal terms. Welcome to robot dynamics.

Consider a 2-DOF planar manipulator with revolute joints, link lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$, masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, and centre-of-mass inertias $I_1$ and $I_2$.

Step 1 — Coordinates. Take $q_1 = \theta_1$ as the angle of the first link relative to the base, and $q_2 = \theta_2$ as the angle of the second link relative to the first.

Step 2 — Kinetic energy. Each link contributes translational kinetic energy from its centre-of-mass velocity plus rotational kinetic energy. Link 1 rotates with angular velocity $\dot{\theta}_1$. Link 2 rotates with $\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2$, and its centre of mass has a velocity that mixes both joint rates — so $T$ contains a cross-term in $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$. This cross-term is exactly the inertial coupling between the two joints.

Step 3 — Potential energy. The height of each centre of mass depends on $\theta_1$ (and, for link 2, on $\theta_2$ as well). $V$ is therefore a configuration-dependent sum of gravity terms.

Step 4 — Euler–Lagrange. Apply the equation for $i = 1$ and $i = 2$. You will get two coupled, nonlinear ODEs containing inertial terms, Coriolis/centrifugal terms (from the $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ and $\dot{\theta}_j^2$ structure), and gravitational terms.

Even this minimal example shows the texture of all manipulator dynamics: the inertia matrix is configuration-dependent, the joints are inertially coupled, and gravity loads vary with pose.

Pay attention
Where the coupling enters

Link 2's centre-of-mass velocity depends on both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$. Squaring that velocity in $T$ produces the cross-term $\dot{\theta}_1\dot{\theta}_2$ — the off-diagonal entries of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

First, sweep the elbow angle and watch the $2\times 2$ inertia matrix breathe. The off-diagonal $D_{12}$ should collapse to exactly $m_2 L_2^2$ when link 2 sits perpendicular to link 1 — the special case from homework Task 4.

Then take the wheel yourself. Type a Lagrangian for the 2-DOF arm (or load the homework template), let the playground apply Euler–Lagrange symbolically, and watch the resulting trajectory simulate. Edit a term — the equations and the motion both update.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 05 → 06 —
Sec. №06

Velocity kinematics for energy calculations

Every revolute joint adds itself to every link downstream. Once you see that, you can write angular velocities by inspection.

To turn $T$ into a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, we need explicit expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ in terms of joint velocities.

Linear velocity. If the centre of mass of link $i$ has position $\mathbf{r}_i(\mathbf{q})$, then by the chain rule

$$\mathbf{v}_i = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_1}\dot{q}_1 + \cdots + \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_i}\dot{q}_i = \mathbf{J}_{vi}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}},$$

where $\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ is the linear-velocity Jacobian for that centre of mass.

Angular velocity. For a revolute joint $j$, every link beyond joint $j$ in the chain picks up $\dot{q}_j$ in its angular velocity. Prismatic joints contribute nothing. The total angular velocity of link $i$ is the vector sum of contributions from all revolute joints between the base and link $i$.

For a 3-DOF planar arm: $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1 = \dot{q}_1$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2$, $\boldsymbol{\omega}_3 = \dot{q}_1 + \dot{q}_2 + \dot{q}_3$ — each successive link is driven by more joints, so the kinetic energy gets steadily richer in coupling terms.

Angular velocities of a 3-DOF planar revolute armω₁ = q̇₁
ω₂ = q̇₁ + q̇₂
ω₃ = q̇₁ + q̇₂ + q̇₃
Definition
Two Jacobians per link

$\mathbf{J}_{vi}$ maps $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ to the linear velocity of link $i$'s centre of mass; the rotational Jacobian $\mathbf{J}_{\omega i}$ does the same for $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$.

Build it yourself. Drag joint-rate contributions onto each link until $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1, \boldsymbol{\omega}_2, \boldsymbol{\omega}_3$ pick up exactly the joints upstream of them. The win condition encodes the rule that lets you write angular velocities by inspection.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 06 → 07 —
Sec. №07

Kinetic energy in matrix form: the inertia matrix

The inertia matrix is the kinetic energy's fingerprint. Everything that makes robot dynamics nonlinear lives inside $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

Substituting the Jacobian expressions for $\mathbf{v}_i$ and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_i$ into $T$, the total kinetic energy becomes a quadratic form in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$:

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}\, \dot{\mathbf{q}}^{T} \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{\mathbf{q}},$$

where the inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ has entries

$$D_{ij}(\mathbf{q}) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ m_k \left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^{T}\!\left(\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) + \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_i}\right)^{T} \mathbf{I}_k \left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}_k}{\partial q_j}\right) \right].$$

Reading this physically: $D_{ii}$ is the effective inertia seen by joint $i$ when only joint $i$ moves, while the off-diagonal entries $D_{ij}$ encode inertial coupling between joints. $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is always symmetric and positive definite — symmetry follows from the construction, and positive definiteness follows from the fact that kinetic energy is positive whenever the robot is moving.

The configuration dependence of $\mathbf{D}$ is the reason robot dynamics are nonlinear: as the arm changes posture, the effective inertia changes, and so does the coupling between joints.

Spec
Three properties to remember

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is symmetric, positive definite, and configuration-dependent. The first two guarantee a sane physics; the third is what makes the dynamics nonlinear.

Structure
Diagonal vs off-diagonal

Diagonals = effective inertia of each joint in isolation. Off-diagonals = inertial coupling — torque applied at joint $j$ shows up as acceleration at joint $i$.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 07 → 08 —
Sec. №08

From the Lagrangian to the manipulator equation

The whole module collapses to one line: $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$. Memorise it; we will use it everywhere.

We now apply the Euler–Lagrange equations to $L = T - V$ using $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) \dot{\mathbf{q}}$.

Step 1 — Velocity derivative.

$$\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_i} = \sum_{j} D_{ij}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{q}_j.$$

Step 2 — Take $d/dt$. Because $\mathbf{D}$ depends on $\mathbf{q}$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\!\left(\frac{\partial T}{\partial \dot{q}_i}\right) = \sum_{j} D_{ij}\, \ddot{q}_j + \sum_{j,k} \frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k}\, \dot{q}_k \dot{q}_j.$$

Step 3 — Position derivatives.

$$\frac{\partial T}{\partial q_i} = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{j,k} \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\, \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k, \qquad \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_i} = c_i(\mathbf{q}).$$

Step 4 — Assemble. Substituting into the Euler–Lagrange equation and collecting terms gives, for each $i$,

$$\sum_{j} D_{ij}(\mathbf{q})\, \ddot{q}_j + h_i(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + c_i(\mathbf{q}) = \tau_i,$$

or in compact matrix form

$$\boxed{\;\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}\;}.$$

This is the equation of robot dynamics. Every algorithm in the rest of the course — inverse dynamics, computed-torque control, simulation — is built on it.

Standard formD(q) q̈ + h(q, q̇) + c(q) = τ
Headline result
Standard manipulator equation

$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ — inertia × acceleration, plus velocity-coupling terms, plus gravity, equals applied joint torque.

Drive the derivation yourself, one rule at a time. The widget shows the current expression and a menu of production rules; pick the one Euler–Lagrange actually needs next and the next line unlocks.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 08 → 09 —
Sec. №09

Anatomy of the manipulator equation: $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$

Three terms, three stories: inertia, motion-coupling, gravity. Keep them straight and the equations of motion stop being scary.

The Lagrangian derivation naturally splits the equation of motion into three physically meaningful pieces.

Inertia $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$. Comes from $T$. Symmetric, positive definite, configuration-dependent. Its diagonal entries are the effective inertias of each joint; off-diagonals carry the inertial coupling.

Coriolis and centrifugal terms $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$. Come from the time derivative of $\mathbf{D}$ and from $\partial T/\partial \mathbf{q}$. They are quadratic in joint velocities:

$$h_i(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) = \sum_{j,k} h_{ijk}(\mathbf{q})\, \dot{q}_j \dot{q}_k, \quad h_{ijk} = \tfrac{1}{2}\!\left(\frac{\partial D_{ij}}{\partial q_k} + \frac{\partial D_{ik}}{\partial q_j} - \frac{\partial D_{jk}}{\partial q_i}\right).$$

The symbols $h_{ijk}$ are the Christoffel symbols of the first kind. Terms with $j = k$ are centrifugal (one joint moves, pushing another); terms with $j \neq k$ are Coriolis (two joints moving simultaneously produce a coupling).

Gravity $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$. Comes from $V$:

$$c_i(\mathbf{q}) = \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_i}.$$

This is the static torque the actuator must supply just to hold the arm against gravity at configuration $\mathbf{q}$.

Knowing which physical effect a given term represents is what lets you debug a derivation: if all your velocity-squared terms come out wrong, you have a problem in $\mathbf{h}$; if a stationary pose drifts in simulation, you have a problem in $\mathbf{c}$.

Term 1 of 3
$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ — inertia

Symmetric, positive definite. Comes straight from kinetic energy.

Term 2 of 3
$\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$ — Coriolis / centrifugal

Quadratic in $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$. Built from Christoffel symbols of $\mathbf{D}$. Zero when nothing is moving.

Term 3 of 3
$\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ — gravity

$c_i = \partial V/\partial q_i$. The static load you have to fight just to hold a pose.

Check your grip with four questions. Decide which term carries which physical effect, what vanishes when the robot is stationary, and where to look first when a simulation misbehaves. The distractors are the misreadings most often seen in coursework.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 09 → 10 —
Sec. №10

Why this matters in industry

Everything in Module 2 ends up baked into industrial controllers at 1 kHz. Treat it accordingly.

The Lagrangian formulation is not just a tidy piece of mathematics — it is what runs inside modern industrial robot controllers. Embedded controllers evaluate $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, $\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$, and $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q})$ at 1 kHz or faster and use them for computed-torque control, trajectory optimisation, collision detection by energy monitoring, and predictive maintenance.

A concrete example from automotive welding: a manufacturer replaced simple per-joint PID control with model-based control built on the Lagrangian dynamic model. Position error dropped from $\pm 2$ mm to $\pm 0.2$ mm, cycle times fell from 45 s to 28 s, and energy consumption dropped by around 25%. The whole improvement comes from the controller knowing, at every instant, what torque is needed for inertia, what is needed for Coriolis/centrifugal coupling, and what is needed for gravity — exactly the three terms we just derived.

That is the punchline of this module: the same scalar reasoning we used to write $L = T - V$ on paper is, almost literally, what is doing real-time computation on a factory robot.

Where deployed
Where the equation lives

Computed-torque control, model-predictive control, simulation, energy-based safety monitoring — all built on $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$.

— SHEET BREAK · TRANSITION 10 → 11 —
Sec. №11

Module summary and what comes next

If you can explain why $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric, what $\mathbf{h}$ does when nothing is moving, and where $\mathbf{c}$ comes from, you are ready for Module 3.

We replaced free-body diagrams with energy. We wrote kinetic energy as $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}$, potential energy as $V = \sum m_i \mathbf{g}^T \mathbf{r}_i$, and combined them into the Lagrangian $L = T - V$. The Euler–Lagrange equations then gave us the standard form

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h}(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau},$$

with every term physically meaningful and every step procedural.

Module 3 will take this same machinery and push it further: explicit velocity formulations along the kinematic chain, a systematic algorithm for assembling $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$, computation of the Coriolis/centrifugal block $\mathbf{h}$ via Christoffel symbols, and worked examples on real robot geometries.

Before moving on, make sure you are comfortable with: matrix calculus and partial derivatives of matrix expressions, position and velocity expressions from transformation matrices, dot/cross products and frame transformations, and kinetic and potential energy in multi-body systems.

Self-check
Conceptual check

Can you explain: why energy methods beat force methods for robots, what each term in $\mathbf{D}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} + \mathbf{c} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$ represents, how the Lagrangian handles constraint forces, and why manipulator dynamics are nonlinear and coupled?

Next sheet
Coming in Module 3

Lagrangian formulation for robot dynamics — full derivations for real geometries, velocity Jacobians along the chain, and the assembly of $\mathbf{D}$, $\mathbf{h}$, $\mathbf{c}$ in practice.

Practice — try these on your own

Small activities to test your grip on today's ideas. Try each one first, sketch as you go, then reveal the worked solution to compare. These are formative — nothing to hand in.

1 · Kinematics of a 2-DOF planar arm with tip masses

Consider a 2-link planar arm with revolute joints. Link 1 has length $L_1$ with point mass $m_1$ at its tip; link 2 has length $L_2$ with point mass $m_2$ at its tip. Joint angles $\theta_1$ (link 1 vs the horizontal $x$-axis) and $\theta_2$ (link 2 vs link 1) are measured in the usual way. Neglect distributed link mass and inertia.

Write the position vectors of $m_1$ and $m_2$ in the base frame as functions of $L_1, L_2, \theta_1, \theta_2$. Then differentiate to get their velocities in terms of $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$.

Self-check after you've tried
  • Your $\mathbf{r}_1$ should depend only on $L_1$ and $\theta_1$, not on $\theta_2$.
  • $\mathbf{r}_2$ should be the sum of two vectors of lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$ at angles $\theta_1$ and $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ respectively.
  • After differentiating, $\mathbf{v}_1$ should be linear in $\dot{\theta}_1$; $\mathbf{v}_2$ should be linear in both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$.
Show worked solution

Positions. Tip of link 1:

$$\mathbf{r}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} L_1 \cos\theta_1 \\ L_1 \sin\theta_1 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Tip of link 2 (link 2 is at angle $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ in the base frame):

$$\mathbf{r}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} L_1 \cos\theta_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2) \\ L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2) \end{bmatrix}.$$

Velocities. Differentiating with respect to time:

$$\mathbf{v}_1 = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -L_1 \sin\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 \\ \phantom{-}L_1 \cos\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 \end{bmatrix},$$ $$\mathbf{v}_2 = \dot{\mathbf{r}}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -L_1 \sin\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 - L_2 \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2) \\ \phantom{-}L_1 \cos\theta_1\, \dot{\theta}_1 + L_2 \cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)(\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2) \end{bmatrix}.$$

Notice that $\mathbf{v}_2$ involves both $\dot{\theta}_1$ and $\dot{\theta}_2$ — that coupling is what will produce the off-diagonal entries of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ in the next task.

2 · Kinetic energy and the inertia matrix

Using the velocities you derived in Task 1, write the total kinetic energy $T = \tfrac{1}{2} m_1 \|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 \|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2$ as a quadratic form in $\dot{\theta}_1, \dot{\theta}_2$. Read off the entries of the $2\times 2$ inertia matrix $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$.

Self-check after you've tried
  • $T$ should be a sum of $\dot{\theta}_1^2$, $\dot{\theta}_2^2$, and $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ terms — no other velocity products.
  • $\mathbf{D}$ must be symmetric: $D_{12} = D_{21}$.
  • At $\theta_2 = \pi/2$ (link 2 perpendicular to link 1), $\cos\theta_2 = 0$ and the off-diagonal entry should reduce to $m_2 L_2^2$.
Show worked solution

Squared magnitudes. Since point-mass tips have no rotational kinetic energy of their own, only $\tfrac{1}{2}m_i\|\mathbf{v}_i\|^2$ contributes.

$\|\mathbf{v}_1\|^2 = L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2$.

For $\mathbf{v}_2$, expand and use $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ on the $\theta_1$ and $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ pieces, with cross terms collapsing via $\cos(A)\cos(B) + \sin(A)\sin(B) = \cos(A - B)$:

$$\|\mathbf{v}_2\|^2 = L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + 2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2).$$

Total kinetic energy.

$$T = \tfrac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2).$$

Read off $\mathbf{D}$. Collect coefficients of $\dot{\theta}_1^2$, $\dot{\theta}_2^2$, and $\dot{\theta}_1\dot{\theta}_2$ in $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})\dot{\mathbf{q}}$:

$$\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) = \begin{bmatrix} (m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 + m_2 L_2^2 + 2 m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 & m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 \\ m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2 & m_2 L_2^2 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Note $\mathbf{D}$ is symmetric and depends on $\theta_2$ only — the explicit configuration-dependence of the effective inertia.

3 · Potential energy and the Lagrangian

Take gravity acting in $-y$. Write the gravitational potential energy $V$ of the two tip masses as a function of $\theta_1, \theta_2$. Then form the Lagrangian $L = T - V$ using your $T$ from Task 2.

Self-check after you've tried
  • $V$ should depend on $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ but not on the joint velocities.
  • $V$ should be zero when both link tips sit on the $x$-axis ($\theta_1 = \theta_2 = 0$).
  • Inspect the partial $\partial V/\partial \theta_1$: it should give a gravity-torque term that vanishes when the arm hangs straight down.
Show worked solution

Heights of the tip masses. From the position expressions in Task 1, the $y$-coordinates are

$$y_1 = L_1 \sin\theta_1, \qquad y_2 = L_1 \sin\theta_1 + L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

Potential energy. With $g$ the magnitude of gravity and reference height at $y = 0$,

$$V = m_1 g\, y_1 + m_2 g\, y_2 = (m_1 + m_2) g L_1 \sin\theta_1 + m_2 g L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

Lagrangian. Using $T$ from Task 2,

$$L = T - V = \tfrac{1}{2}(m_1 + m_2) L_1^2 \dot{\theta}_1^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} m_2 L_2^2 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2\, \dot{\theta}_1 (\dot{\theta}_1 + \dot{\theta}_2)$$ $$\qquad - (m_1 + m_2) g L_1 \sin\theta_1 - m_2 g L_2 \sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2).$$

This Lagrangian is everything the Euler–Lagrange machinery needs. From here, applying $\frac{d}{dt}(\partial L/\partial \dot{\theta}_i) - \partial L/\partial \theta_i = \tau_i$ for $i = 1, 2$ produces the two coupled equations of motion of the 2-DOF arm.

4 · Verify symmetry and a special case of $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$

Take the inertia matrix from Task 2 and verify two things by hand: (a) $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})$ is symmetric for all $\theta_2$, and (b) when $\theta_2 = \pm \pi/2$, the inertial coupling $D_{12}$ reduces to a purely geometric expression in $m_2$ and $L_2$ — write down what it becomes and explain physically why the $L_1$ contribution disappears in that pose.

Self-check after you've tried
  • After substituting $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, you should get $D_{12} = m_2 L_2^2$.
  • The disappearance of $L_1$ must be tied to the geometry of link 2's velocity contribution from joint 1 in that pose — try sketching the arm at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$.
  • Symmetry should follow from the construction of $T$ as $\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D} \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ — there is no way to tell $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ apart from $\dot{\theta}_2 \dot{\theta}_1$.
Show worked solution

(a) Symmetry. From Task 2,

$$D_{12}(\mathbf{q}) = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2, \qquad D_{21}(\mathbf{q}) = m_2 L_2^2 + m_2 L_1 L_2 \cos\theta_2.$$

These are identical for every $\theta_2$, so $\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{D}(\mathbf{q})^T$. Symmetry is structural: $T = \tfrac{1}{2}\dot{\mathbf{q}}^T \mathbf{D}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ only sees the symmetric part of $\mathbf{D}$, so we can — and do — take $\mathbf{D}$ symmetric without loss of generality.

(b) Special case $\theta_2 = \pi/2$. Then $\cos\theta_2 = 0$, and

$$D_{12} = m_2 L_2^2 + 0 = m_2 L_2^2.$$

The physical picture: at $\theta_2 = \pi/2$, link 2 sticks out perpendicular to link 1. When joint 1 moves, the component of $m_2$'s motion that is aligned with the motion driven by joint 2 reduces to the motion at distance $L_2$ from joint 2's axis — the $L_1$ contribution to $\mathbf{v}_2$ is perpendicular to the joint-2 contribution and so does not couple into the $\dot{\theta}_1 \dot{\theta}_2$ cross-term.

In short: the off-diagonal of $\mathbf{D}$ measures how much joint 1's motion helps joint 2's motion in $T$. At $\theta_2 = \pi/2$ that overlap is purely $m_2 L_2^2$, the same value as $D_{22}$ itself.
